Avodah Zarah 68b:11.english: The Gemara recounts an incident involving a certain mouse that fell into a barrel of beer. Rav deemed that barrel of beer forbidden. The Sages said before Rav Sheshet: Shall we say that Rav maintains that even in a case where the forbidden substance imparts flavor to the detriment of the mixture, it is forbidden? For the mouse's taste certainly detracts!

Avodah Zarah 68b:15.english: Rather, what have you to say? With regard to the ritual impurity of semen, the Merciful One states in the verse: “The flow of seed” (Leviticus 15:16), meaning that the reference is to semen that is fit to fertilize. Here too, with regard to the ritual impurity of a mouse, the verse states: “When they have died” (Leviticus 11:32). The Merciful One states that the carcasses of creeping animals impart impurity only when they are similar to the creeping animals' state at time of their death, i.e., when they are still moist. Therefore, there is no contradiction to the claim that the prohibition against eating a mouse is a novelty and consequently applies even when it detracted from the flavor of the food into which it fell.

Avodah Zarah 69a:1.english: If a mouse fell into vinegar, what is the halakha? Does the mouse enhance its flavor? Rav Hillel said to Rav Ashi: There was such an incident in the study hall of Rav Kahana, and Rav Kahana deemed the vinegar forbidden. This indicates that it enhances the flavor. Rav Ashi said to him: This is not a proof. That mouse was dismembered, and Rav Kahana deemed the vinegar forbidden due to concern that one might consume a substantive piece of the mouse in the vinegar, which is prohibited regardless of the taste.

Avodah Zarah 69a:5.english: MISHNA: With regard to a gentile who was transporting barrels of wine from one place to another place together with a Jew, if the wine was under the presumption of being supervised, it is permitted. But if the Jew notified the gentile that the Jew was going far away, the wine is forbidden if the Jew left for a sufficient amount of time for the gentile to bore a hole [sheyishtom] in the barrel, seal the barrel again with plaster, and for the plaster to dry. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: The wine is forbidden only if it was sufficient time for the gentile to open the barrel by removing the stopper altogether, stop the barrel again by making a new stopper, and for the new stopper to dry.

Avodah Zarah 69a:6.english: With regard to one who placed his wine in a wagon or on a ship with a gentile, and went on his way by a shortcut [bekappendarya], such that the gentile does not know when the Jew will encounter the gentile, even if the Jew entered the city and bathed, the wine is permitted, because the gentile would not use the wine for a libation, for fear the owner might catch the gentile at it.

Avodah Zarah 69a:7.english: If the Jew informed the gentile that the Jew was going away for a long period of time, the wine is forbidden if it was sufficient time for the gentile to bore a hole in the barrel, seal it again with plaster, and for the plaster to dry. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: It is forbidden only if it was sufficient time for the gentile to open the barrel by removing the stopper altogether, stop the barrel again, and for the new stopper to dry.

Avodah Zarah 69a:8.english: With regard to one who left a gentile in the Jew's shop, even if the Jew went out and came in and was not there all the time, the wine is permitted. But if the Jew informed the gentile that the Jew was going away for a long period of time, the wine is forbidden if it was sufficient time for the gentile to bore a hole in the barrel, seal it again with plaster, and for the plaster to dry. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: The wine is forbidden only if it was sufficient time for the gentile to open the barrel, stop the barrel again, and for the new stopper to dry.

Avodah Zarah 69a:9.english: If a Jew was eating with a gentile at the table, and left jugs [laginin] of wine on the table and a jug on the side table [hadulebaki], and the Jew left the gentile and went out, what is on the table is forbidden, as it is likely that the gentile handled the wine, whereas what is on the side table is permitted. But if the Jew said to the gentile: Mix water with the wine and the gentile may drink, even the jug that is on the side table is forbidden. Similarly, open barrels are forbidden, but sealed barrels are permitted unless the Jew was out of the room for sufficient time for the gentile to open the barrel by removing the stopper, and stop the barrel again by making a new stopper, and for the new stopper to dry.

Otzar La'azei Rashi, Talmud, Avodah Zara.english:
1906 / (Avodah Zarah 69a.) / Mouse
אישקורי"ל / squirrel / Squirrel
Here, in contrast to Sanhedrin 91a. (above, no. 1722), it is not a common mouse, but a field mouse. But even a field mouse is different from our squirrel.
✭ squirrel

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:12:1.hebrew: והכא - גבי שרץ, היינו טעמא דאסור בפגם:
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:12:1.english: But here - With regard to a creeping animal, that is the reason it is forbidden even if it imparts a detrimental flavor:

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:12:2.english: As it is - The prohibition of a creeping animal is a novelty:

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:12:3.hebrew: דהא מימאיס - ובלאו אזהרה, בדילין אינשי מיניה. ולמה ליה דאזהר רחמנא עליה? שמע מינה: אפילו נותן טעם לפגם אסור:
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:12:3.english: As it is repulsive - And without a warning, people distance themselves from it. So why did the Merciful One warn about it? Learn from this: Even if it imparts a detrimental flavor, it is forbidden:

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:13:1.english: If that is so - If it is a novelty:

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:13:2.hebrew: יטמא לח ויבש - שהרי מאוס הוא, ובדילי אינשי ממגעו. למה ליה דאזהר רחמנא עליה? שמע מינה: אפילו כשהוא יבש מטמא:
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:13:2.english: It should impart ritual impurity whether moist or dried out - For it is repulsive, and people distance themselves from touching it. Why did the Merciful One warn about it? Learn from this: Even when it is dry, it imparts impurity:

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:13:3.hebrew: אלמה תנן - במסכת נדה (דף נד:): "אבל השרץ ושכבת זרע מטמאין לחין ואין מטמאין יבשין". אלא לאו שמע מינה: לא מאיס שרץ ולאו חידוש, ואיצטריך לאזהורי עליה דעובדי כוכבים אכלי:
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:13:3.english: Why did we learn - In Tractate Niddah (page 54b): "But a creeping animal and semen impart impurity when moist but do not impart impurity when dry." Rather, must we not conclude from this: A creeping animal is not repulsive, and it is not a novelty, and it was necessary to warn about it because gentiles eat it:

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:14:1.hebrew: וליטעמיך שכבת זרע - הא ודאי ממאיס, ובדילי אינשי ממגעו, וחידוש הוא, תטמא לח ויבש:
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:14:1.english: And according to your reasoning, semen - This is certainly repulsive, and people distance themselves from touching it, and it is a novelty, so it should impart impurity whether moist or dried out:

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:15:1.hebrew: אלא - שאני לענין טומאה, אע"ג דחידוש הוא, גזירת הכתוב היא דלח ולא יבש, דכתיב: "כל אשר יפול עליו מהם במותם", כעין מותם, כשהן לחין:
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:15:1.english: Rather - It is different concerning ritual impurity. Even though it is a novelty, it is a decree of the verse that it is impure when moist but not when dry, as it is written: "whatever any of them falls upon, when they are dead" (Leviticus 11:32), meaning similar to their death, when they are moist:

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:15:2.hebrew: שכבת זרע אמר רחמנא בראויה להזריע - "או איש אשר תצא ממנו שכבת זרע":
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:15:2.english: The Merciful One states "semen" concerning that which is fit to fertilize - "When a man has an emission of semen" (Leviticus 15:16):

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:16:1.english: A city mouse - A mouse from a settlement is repulsive:

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:16:2.english: A field mouse - écureuil in Old French:

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:11:1.english: What is different in the first clause and what is different in the latter clause? - Surely, they see them touching, as it states that they were laden with ritually pure items, and these are not sealed barrels.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:11:2.english: By purifying his donkey drivers: - That he immersed them, and their touch is ritually pure.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:12:1.english: About contact with another: - With another am ha'aretz who encounters him on the way and was not purified for this purpose.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:12:2.english: Even in the first clause: - Since he went far away, there is reason to be concerned about this.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:1:1.hebrew: נפל לגו חלא מאי - מי אמרינן: החומץ טעמו קשה, ואין השרץ מפיגו לתת בו טעם?
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:1:1.english: If it fell into vinegar, what is the halakha? Do we say: The vinegar has a strong taste, and the creeping animal does not detract from it to impart a flavor?

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:1:2.hebrew: אימרטוטי אימרטט - לחתיכות דקות קטנות, ושרץ איסורו בכעדשה כטומאתו, וחיישינן דלמא בולע חתיכות שרץ בהדי חומץ:
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:1:2.english: It was dismembered - Into small, thin pieces. And the prohibition of a creeping animal is with a lentil-sized amount, like its impurity, and we are concerned that one might swallow pieces of the creeping animal along with the vinegar:

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:3:1.hebrew: בחמשין - כיון דחומץ טעמו קשה, לא בעי שתין לבטוליה, דאפילו בחמשין לא יהיב ביה טעמא:
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:3:1.english: At fifty - Since vinegar has a strong taste, it does not require sixty to nullify it, for even at fifty, it does not impart its flavor:

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:4:1.hebrew: ה"ג וכן כל איסור שבתורה - בששים. וכן הלכה רווחת בישראל: דמין בשאינו מינו בששים, חוץ מחמץ. אבל מין במינו מוקמינן בפסחים (דף ל.): הלכתא במשהו כרב, וטעמא משום דכל איסורין שבתורה מין במינו במשהו כרב, ובחמץ גזירה שאינו מינו אטו מינו:
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:4:1.english: This is how it is taught: And so is the ruling for all prohibitions in the Torah - With sixty. And so is the widespread halakha in Israel: that a substance of one kind in a mixture not of its kind is nullified by sixty, except for ḥametz. But a substance of its own kind, we establish in Pesahim (page 30a): The halakha is that it is nullified by any amount, like Rav. And the reason is that all prohibitions in the Torah, a substance of its own kind is nullified by any amount, like Rav. And with ḥametz, it is a decree that a substance not of its kind is like a substance of its own kind:

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:5:1.english: If it was under the presumption of being supervised - The Gemara explains that even though the Jew went far away from the gentile by a mil, if the Jew did not inform the gentile that the Jew was going far away, the wine is permitted, because the gentile is always afraid that the Jew might come now.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:5:2.english: And if he notified him that he was going far away - that the Jew was distancing himself, and the barrels were sealed.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:5:3.english: Its measure is for him to bore a hole, seal it, and dry it - If the Jew remained away for enough time for the gentile to bore a hole in the barrel's stopper, and then reseal the hole, and for the sealing to dry, the wine is forbidden.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:5:4.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says - The wine is not forbidden unless the Jew remains away for enough time for the gentile to open the entire stopper of the barrel, and it is impossible to remove the stopper without breaking it completely.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:5:5.english: And stop it - and the gentile makes another new stopper.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:5:6.english: And dry - and the stopper dries, but for boring a hole, the Sages were not concerned because it is noticeable. And shetom is like the expression shetom ha'ayin (Numbers 24:3), an open eye that sees well.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:6:1.english: One who placed his wine in a wagon or on a ship - with the gentile.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:6:2.english: And went - the Jew by a shortcut.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:6:3.english: And entered the city and bathed - in the bathhouse, the wine is permitted, since the gentile did not know that the Jew was delayed, the gentile was afraid and did not touch the wine.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:9:2.english: What is on the table is forbidden - because the gentile will say: This Jew invited me to eat and drink, and the gentile touched the wine.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:9:3.english: What is on the side table is permitted - because it is not prepared for this meal.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:9:4.english: And if he said to him: Mix and drink - Since the Jew strengthened the gentile's hands with some permission, the gentile's mind is at ease, and the gentile touched all of the wine.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:9:5.english: Open barrels - in the house are forbidden.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:9:6.english: Sealed barrels are permitted - until the Jew remains away for enough time for the gentile to open, stop, and dry, and the anonymous Mishna follows Rabban Shimon since it does not state 'to bore a hole'.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69b:1:1.english: When he comes to them by a roundabout way: - When the owner can come by a roundabout way, so that the gentile is afraid, thinking: 'Now he will come!'

Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 104:1.english:
On the Presence of a Rat in Wine or Beer
In a mixture, the dormouse gives a pleasant flavor: previously, moreover, important people regarded it as a delicacy. It is not known if the rat, which lives in dwellings, alters or improves the flavor of wine and vinegar. When a rat falls into vinegar or cold beer, this liquid is permitted if, within twenty-four hours, the rat is removed whole. But if the same liquid is hot or cold and the rat is removed whole or in pieces after a stay of twenty-four hours, the liquid is permitted if it can be filtered, contains no trace of the rat, and is sixty times greater in volume than the animal.
GLOSS: Only the presence of an insect is to be feared, not that of other forbidden things.

Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 129:1.english:
Wine left in a place where a gentile is present and a Jew enters at every moment.
Wine is permitted, even if a Jew left a gentile alone in the place where the liquid is located, whether in a store, on a vessel, or in a wagon; the Jew may even be absent to go to the synagogue or any house. The same applies when a gentile transported a barrel of wine from one place to another during the absence of the Jew, who left the gentile alone where the wine was.
GLOSS: It is forbidden to deliberately leave wine or vinegar in a gentile's house if the gentile lives alone; but if it has already happened, the wine is permitted. The wine is also permitted when the transport occurred during the absence of the Jew who had entrusted its custody to a gentile, because the latter fears the sudden arrival of the Jew. In all cases, one must be unaware of what the gentile may have done, i.e., whether he closed the door or moved the wagon or vessel to hide from view.
The wine is also permitted, even if the gentile closed the door of the store, if it has a crack or a hole allowing one to see everything that happens inside; this case is assimilated to that of an open door. The wine is permitted only if there is a roundabout path that allows the Jew to return suddenly, without the gentile being able to see him; the same applies when the Jew went to the bathhouse. When the Jew entered a bathhouse, to the knowledge of the gentile, who then knows perfectly well that the Jew will be absent for a long time; or when the Jew told the gentile: «Guard the wine in my store», because the gentile then understood that the Jew was to go away; or when he told the gentile: «Transport the barrel of wine to such and such a place, I will return afterwards»; when the Jew announced to the gentile that he was separating from him, all barrels of wine are forbidden if they are open; if they are sealed, and if the Jew went far enough away to give the gentile time to open them and close them with clay or lime and make any trace of moisture disappear, they are all forbidden.
GLOSS: Some authors claim that wine contained in closed and sealed barrels is always permitted, because one seal is sufficient for a barrel of wine; this opinion can be accepted when the loss caused by the prohibition would be significant.

Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 129:7.english: When a Jew and a gentile are sitting and each drinking their own wine, when the former hears that he is being called to go to the synagogue; he goes to pray and leaves his wine there: it remains permitted, if there is a roundabout path allowing the Jew to unexpectedly return to the place where he left the gentile. But if the wine remained on the table, while another wine was placed at a certain distance from the furniture, the first is forbidden if the gentile remained alone; the second is also forbidden, if it was placed within reach of the gentile's hand; but it is permitted, if the distance separating it from the gentile did not allow the latter to touch it by extending his hand. When a Jew told a gentile to mix water with wine to make a drink, all barrels filled with this liquid, which were in the house and were open, are forbidden; those that were closed are permitted, provided, however, that the gentile did not remain alone for a long enough time to allow him to open and close the barrels with clay or lime and make any trace of moisture disappear.

Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 92:1.english:
Milk Falling into a Meat Pot
When a piece of meat the size of an olive falls into a container of hot milk, the milk is tasted by a gentile; if he detects the taste of meat, the milk is forbidden; otherwise, it is permitted, even if it does not present a quantity sixty times greater than the meat. But the piece of meat is forbidden. However, this is only if the piece of meat was extracted before it had released the absorbed milk, i.e., it was extracted before the boiling ceased; but if it was extracted later, even if the gentile detects no meat taste when tasting it, it is forbidden unless it presents a quantity sixty times greater than the meat.
GLOSS: See further, § 98, where it is said that we do not rely on a gentile's tasting, and therefore, we always require a quantity sixty times greater.

Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 98:1.english:
On the Mixing of Forbidden Food with Permitted Food and Dissolution
When a forbidden food is mixed with a permitted food of a different nature, for example, when forbidden fat is mixed with meat, the mixture must be tasted by a gentile. If the gentile says that they do not detect the flavor of the forbidden food, or if they do detect it but find it altered, the mixture is permitted, provided that the forbidden food has not subsequently improved the taste of the mixture; but the gentile must not be made aware that their opinion is needed. If there is no gentile to taste the mixture, the permitted food must be sixty times the amount of the forbidden food. The same applies to a mixture of two foods, one forbidden and one permitted, but both of the same nature, making tasting ineffective; in this case, the permitted food must be sixty times the forbidden food.
GLOSS: Nowadays it is customary not to have the mixture tasted by a gentile; it suffices to evaluate if the quantity of the permitted food is sixty times that of the forbidden food.

Steinsaltz comment #1 on Avodah Zarah 69.english: The Rishonim found this difficult: Ostensibly, from the continuation of the passage — "But if the Jew notified him that he was going far away" — it implies that as long as the Jew did not notify the gentile, the wine is considered supervised. So what is the place for this question? From Rashi's words, it appears that the question is in a case where the Jew did not notify the gentile that he was going far away, to what extent can we consider the gentile's lack of knowledge as a reliable factor. Indeed, Tosafot explained that precisely from the precise wording of the continuation, "if the Jew notified him that he was going far away," it implies that these barrels have a special presumption of supervision, in addition to the fact that the Jew did not notify the gentile that he was going far away. The conclusion of the matter, according to the discussion in the Baraita, is that the Jew can come by a roundabout way, so that the gentile fears that the Jew might arrive at any moment (Tosafot). The Ramban has a different interpretation regarding this matter; he explains that our Mishna permitted in this case where the Jew did not notify the gentile, even with open barrels. And regarding this, the Gemara asks: How can it be said that wine is presumed to be supervised, such that the gentile does not touch it, when the gentile is carrying an open barrel of wine and the Jew does not see him? Surely the gentile can see the Jew approaching and remove his hand! To this, the answer was that there can be a presumption of supervision — by a roundabout way, where the gentile cannot see the Jew arriving.

Rashi explains: Since this is not discussing sealed barrels as in our Mishna, but rather ritually pure items (which, according to his understanding, refers to someone carrying fruits and the like), they immediately become impure through the donkey drivers, even if the owner did not notify them that he was going far away. And the Ritv'a wrote that according to Rashi's words, the question should not be understood literally, but rather in the sense: What is the reason it is permitted in the first clause? Surely it is clear that these pure items become impure. But Tosafot explained that this is not discussing fruits, but rather open barrels that contained ritually pure items. And for this reason, it is not sufficient in this case for the owner to notify them that he is going far away, as in our Mishna which deals with sealed barrels. Therefore, as soon as they are out of the owner's sight, they are forbidden, even if there was not enough time for the gentile to bore a hole, etc.

Barrels of wine that were left with a gentile are permitted if there is a roundabout way that the owner can come upon the gentile without the gentile being seen in advance, in accordance with the statement of Rava. The Rashba rules that this applies when the gentile is alone, but if there are two or more gentiles the wine is forbidden, as one of them can be on the lookout while the other tampers with the wine (Shulĥan Arukh, Yoreh De’a 129:1–2).

Steinsaltz comment #2 on Avodah Zarah 69.english: If one’s donkey drivers and laborers were amei ha’aretz and were laden with ritually pure items and were walking in front of the owner, even if they went more than a mil ahead of the owner — these items are pure, because they are presumed to be under the owner's supervision, and the donkey drivers and laborers are afraid to touch them, saying: The owner will come now, he is right behind us. This refers, according to Rava, to a case where the owner can go by a roundabout way, so that the donkey drivers and laborers do not know when the owner will come (Kesef Mishneh). But if the owner said to them: Go, and I will come after you, then once they are out of the owner's sight, the items are impure (Rambam, Sefer Tahara, Hilkhot Metamei Mishkav UMoshav 13:5).

Steinsaltz comment #3 on Avodah Zarah 69.english: If one’s donkey drivers and laborers were unreliable with regard to ritual impurity [amei ha’aretz] and they were laden with wine or produce that was pure, and they were walking in front of the owner, even if they moved more than one mil ahead of the owner, the items are still considered pure. This is because the workers are presumed to be under the owner's supervision, and they are afraid to touch the wine or produce, thinking the owner will come upon them at any moment. This applies where the road is a roundabout one, such that they cannot know when the owner will come upon them. If the owner said to them: Go ahead and I will come behind you, the moment they are out of the owner's sight the items are rendered impure (Rambam Sefer Tahara, Hilkhot Metamei Mishkav UMoshav 13:5 and Kesef Mishne there).

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 68b:11.english: It is related: A certain mouse that fell into a barrel of beer. Rav deemed that beer forbidden. The Sages said before Rav Sheshet: Shall we say that Rav maintains that even in a case where the forbidden substance imparts flavor to the detriment of the mixture, it is forbidden? For the mouse's taste certainly detracts!

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 68b:12.english: Rav Sheshet said to them: Rav generally maintains that if the forbidden substance imparts flavor to the detriment of the mixture, it is permitted. But here, in the case of a mouse and similar creatures, it is a unique novelty that the Torah introduced, as it is repulsive and people distance themselves from it on their own. And even so, the Merciful One prohibited it. Therefore, even if it imparts flavor to the detriment of the mixture, it is still forbidden, unlike what we learned from an animal carcass.

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 68b:13.english: The Sages said to Rav Sheshet: If that is so, according to your explanation that it is a novelty and comes to be more stringent than other prohibitions, then the mouse and similar creatures should impart ritual impurity whether they are moist or dried out. Why did we learn in a mishna: Carcasses of creeping animals impart impurity when they are moist but do not impart impurity when they are dried out?

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 68b:14.english: Rav Sheshet said to them: And according to your reasoning, by which you compare the law of ritual impurity to the law of forbidden foods, semen, which is also repulsive, should impart impurity whether moist or dried out. Why did we learn in a mishna: With regard to semen and creeping animals, they impart impurity when they are moist but do not impart impurity when they are dried out?

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 68b:15.english: Rather, what do you have to say? The Merciful One states: "Semen" (Leviticus 15:16). That is to say, it is a Torah decree that it imparts impurity only when it is moist, when it is fit to fertilize. Here too, regarding a mouse and similar creatures, the Merciful One states: "When they have died" (Leviticus 11:32) – meaning that they impart impurity only similar to their death, as they were at the time of their death. Therefore, when they are dry, they no longer impart impurity. And from this, there is no contradiction to the statement that the prohibition against eating a mouse is a novelty and it is forbidden even when it imparts a detrimental flavor.

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 68b:16.english: Rav Shimi of Neharde’a objects to this assumption that we raised: And is the mouse repulsive? But isn’t it served at the table of kings, considered by them a choice food! Rav Shimi of Neharde’a said: This is not difficult. This statement, that a mouse is served as a delicacy, is stated with regard to a field mouse, which is served at the table of kings, and that statement, that it is repulsive, is stated with regard to a city mouse, which is repulsive to everyone.

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 68b:17.english: Rava said: The halakha is that if the forbidden substance imparts flavor to the detriment of the mixture, it is permitted. But with regard to a mouse that fell into beer, I do not know what Rav's reason was for prohibiting it. Is it because he maintains that generally, if the forbidden substance imparts flavor to the detriment of the mixture, it is forbidden, and the halakha is not in accordance with his opinion? Or is it because he maintains that generally, if the forbidden substance imparts flavor to the detriment of the mixture, it is permitted, but a mouse that falls into beer enhances its flavor, and therefore it is forbidden?

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 68b:18.english: A dilemma was raised before them (the students):

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 69a:1.english: It is related: If a mouse fell into vinegar, what is its law? Rav Hillel said to Rav Ashi: There was such an incident in the house of Rav Kahana, and Rav Kahana prohibited that vinegar. From this, it is inferred that it imparts an enhancing flavor and disqualifies the mixture. Rav Ashi said to him: There is no proof from there. That mouse was dismembered into small pieces, and Rav Kahana prohibited it due to the concern that one might come to eat an actual piece of the mouse within the vinegar.

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 69a:10.english: In the explanation of the Mishna, they clarify: What are the circumstances [how exactly is it] of "under the presumption of being supervised"? And they explain: As it is taught [as it is stated in a Baraita]: If one’s donkey drivers and laborers, who were amei ha’aretz and presumed to be ritually impure, were laden with ritually pure items (wine or produce that was prepared in ritual purity), and he warns them not to touch them, but he does not know if they did so or not, even if he went away from them more than a mil — his pure items are pure, as we say that since he warned them, they are afraid of him. But if he said to them: "Go and I will come after you," so that they knew he was not going with them, then once he is out of their sight and no longer sees them — his pure items are impure.

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 69a:11.english: And they ask: What is different in the first clause [how is the beginning, in the first case, different] that if the owner went far away — his pure items are pure, and what is different in the latter clause [and how is the end different] that after the owner's eyes were out of sight — the items are impure? Rav Yitzḥak said: The first clause [at the beginning] discusses a case where the owner purified his donkey drivers and laborers for this, meaning that the owner ensured they immersed, so that they would not render the pure items impure, and therefore there is no concern about their touch.

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 69a:12.english: And they ask: If that is so, in the latter clause also, since the owner purified them for this purpose, why should we be concerned that they rendered the items impure? And they answer: An am ha’aretz is not punctilious about contact with another am ha'aretz. Even though they themselves were ritually pure, perhaps they encountered another am ha’aretz on the way, and the pure items were rendered impure by him, and they are not punctilious about this. And they ask: If that is so, if you are concerned about this, then let us say so even in the first clause!

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 69a:2.english: It is related: Ravina thought to calculate the amount of vinegar necessary to nullify the mouse at 101 times its volume. He said: It should not be worse, meaning, it is not more stringent, than teruma, as we learned in a mishna: Teruma is nullified in a mixture by 101 times its volume. Rav Taḥlifa bar Giza said to Ravina: Perhaps this case is similar to spice of teruma in a pot, whose flavor is not nullified by 101 times its volume, but by more than that!

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 69a:3.english: It is further related: Rav Aḥai calculated the amount of vinegar necessary to nullify the mouse at fifty times its volume. He held that sharp-tasting vinegar does not require sixty times the volume, like other prohibitions in the Torah, to nullify the mouse's flavor. And Rav Shmuel, son of Rav Ika, calculated the amount of beer necessary for nullifying the mouse at sixty times the volume of the mouse.

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 69a:4.english: And they conclude: And the halakha is: This and that, both are nullified by sixty times its volume, and so is the ruling for all prohibitions in the Torah, generally nullified by sixty.

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 69b:1.english: When the owner comes to them by a roundabout way (winding), meaning the owner can come by a crooked, circuitous path, in a way that the donkey drivers and laborers cannot know from where the owner is coming, and therefore they are afraid. And they respond: If that is so, [if such a case is being discussed], then in the latter clause also, why should it not be said that they are afraid? And they respond: Since the owner said to them: "Go and I will come after you," their minds are at ease that the owner will not surprise them.

Tosafot on Avodah Zarah 68b:11:1.hebrew: ההוא עכברא דנפל בגו חביתא דשיכרא אסריה רב לההוא שיכרא - תימה: דהא צונן בצונן הוא ולשתרי? וי"ל דמיירי ששהה שם יום או יומיים, והיה כבוש בתוך השכר, וכבוש הרי הוא כמבושל:
Tosafot on Avodah Zarah 68b:11:1.english: A certain mouse that fell into a barrel of beer, Rav deemed that beer forbidden - It is astonishing: For it is a cold item in a cold item, and it should be permitted! One can say that it refers to a case where it remained there for a day or two, and was pickled in the beer, and a pickled item is considered as if it was cooked.

Tosafot on Avodah Zarah 68b:17:1.hebrew: אמר רבא: הלכתא נותן טעם לפגם כו' - פירוש: אף בשרצים. ולא תימא דבשרצים חידוש כדקאמר לעיל, וליתסר משום פגם דשרצים, אלא אף בשרצים פגם מותר. ועכברא בשיכרא דאסר, לא ידענא אי משום נותן טעם לפגם דקסבר אסור [אף בשאר שרצים], ולית הלכתא כוותיה; פירוש: דאף בשאר שרצים פגם מותר. אי משום דאשבוחי קמשבח. וא"ת: וליפשוט ליה טעמיה דרב מההיא דפרק קמא דחולין (דף ח: ושם ד"ה השוחט): "השוחט בסכין של עובדי כוכבים, רב אמר קולף ושמואל אמר מדיח", ואע"ג דסתם כלי עובדי כוכבים אינם בני יומן, דהשתא הוי לפגם. וי"ל דהתם מיירי בידוע שנשתמשו בו ביום. א"נ, התם טעמא משום שמנונית דאיסור הנדבק בדופני הסכין, שהוא בעין והוי לשבח גם כשאינו בן יומו. וא"ת: מאי קאמר הכא "לא ידענא אי אשבוחי משבח"? ליטעמיה קפילא ארמאה! וי"ל דשמא עכברא בשיכרא מחזק את השכר ומחמצו, והשתא כשנתחזק השכר, אין ידוע אם מחמת השכר עצמו. וקי"ל כרבא דאמר נותן טעם לפגם מותר אף בשרצים, ונפקא מינה דכשאינו בת יומו וכיוצא בו מותר אף בשרצים:
Tosafot on Avodah Zarah 68b:17:1.english: Rava said: The halakha is that if the forbidden substance imparts flavor to its detriment, etc. - This means even with creeping animals. And do not say that with creeping animals it is a novelty, as stated above, and it should be forbidden due to the detrimental flavor of creeping animals. Rather, even with creeping animals, a detrimental flavor is permitted. And regarding the mouse in beer that Rav prohibited, I do not know if it is because he holds that imparting a detrimental flavor is forbidden [even with other creeping animals], and the halakha is not in accordance with his opinion; meaning, that even with other creeping animals, a detrimental flavor is permitted. Or if it is because it enhances the flavor. And if you ask: Why doesn't he resolve Rav's reasoning from that which is stated in the first chapter of Hullin (page 8b, and there, s.v. HaShochet): "One who slaughters with a gentile's knife, Rav says one must peel, and Shmuel says one must rinse," even though gentile's vessels are usually not bat yoma, so it would be detrimental. One can say that there it deals with a case where it is known that it was used on that day. Alternatively, there the reason is due to the fatty residue of the forbidden substance clinging to the sides of the knife, which is tangible and enhances the flavor even when it is not bat yoma. And if you ask: What does he mean here by "I do not know if it enhances the flavor"? Let an Aramaic taster taste it! One can say that perhaps the mouse in beer strengthens the beer and makes it sour, and now that the beer is strengthened, it is not known if it is due to the beer itself. And we rule in accordance with Rava, who says that imparting a detrimental flavor is permitted even with creeping animals, and the practical implication is that when it is not bat yoma and similar cases, it is permitted even with creeping animals:

Tosafot on Avodah Zarah 69a:10:1.english: What are the circumstances described by the phrase: Under the presumption of being supervised? As it is taught: If one’s donkey drivers, etc. - This is established as a case where the owner comes to them by a roundabout way, and here too, it is a case where the owner can come by a roundabout way. And it is a wonder: What is the question, "What are the circumstances"? Surely, from the latter clause which teaches, "But if he notified them that he was going far away," it implies that the first clause is where he did not notify them that he was going far away, and that is the presumption of supervision for him! And it can be said that, on the contrary, from the latter clause which teaches, "But if he notified them, it is forbidden," it implies that if so, the first clause, which teaches "under the presumption of being supervised," means that this supervision is more significant than merely not notifying them that he was going far away. And if it means, for example, [that he did not] notify them that he was going far away, the Mishna should have been silent about the phrase "under the presumption of being supervised," and we would have learned it from the implication of the latter clause. Rather, it certainly comes to say that even if he did not notify them that he was going far away, there is reason to be concerned about the matter, since the gentile sees the Jew moving away. And know that another presumption of supervision is needed, and the Gemara asks what it is, and answers: As it is taught, etc., for example, that the owner can come upon them by a roundabout way.

Tosafot on Avodah Zarah 69a:11:1.english: What is different in the first clause and what is different in the latter clause? - This means: In the first clause, why are his pure items not impure as in the latter clause? And if you say: Let him answer that the first clause deals with a case where he did not notify them that he was going far away, and therefore it is permitted, as it is taught: If he left it under the presumption of being supervised, it is permitted, and this is when he did not notify them that he was going far away. Rashi answered that it is not similar to our Mishna, for this Baraita deals with ritually pure items, such as fruits that he holds in his hands and touches at all times. Therefore, the Gemara asks why there is no distinction. Nevertheless, it is difficult: Let us establish it as referring to barrels, and there would be no difficulty, for 'ritually pure items' can also mean items in barrels. Furthermore, it is difficult: If it deals, as Rashi explained, then the Gemara should not have asked from the first clause to the latter clause, but rather should have asked directly from the first clause itself: What is the reason that in the first clause his pure items are pure, since he holds them and touches them, as Rashi explained? Therefore, it seems to Rabbi Yitzchak that it always deals with barrels, but with open ones that are easy to touch. For this reason, he cannot answer by saying that he did not notify them that he was going far away; nevertheless, it should be forbidden, and it is not similar to our Mishna, which permits wine when he did not notify them that he was going far away, for our Mishna deals with sealed barrels. And if you say: Let us still establish it as referring to sealed barrels, like our Mishna, and there would be no difficulty between the first and latter clauses. It can be said that the Baraita cannot be established as referring to sealed barrels, because it teaches: Once they are out of his sight, his pure items are impure. But if it were sealed barrels, we would require enough time for him to bore a hole, seal it, and for the seal to dry, even if he notified them that he was going far away, as our Mishna teaches.

Tosafot on Avodah Zarah 69a:1:1.hebrew: איבעיא להו: נפל לגו חלא כו' - וא"ת: מ"ש משאר איסורין כמו בשיכרא? וי"ל: משום דחלא חזק מאד, ואגב חורפיה נותן טעם לשבח כמו גבי חילתית. או דלמא מעט השרץ נגד המשקה, וא"כ אין לנו לאסור כל כך. ולכך היה שואל: מה יהיה ממנו?
Tosafot on Avodah Zarah 69a:1:1.english: A dilemma was raised before them: If it fell into vinegar, etc. - And if you ask: What is the difference from other forbidden substances, like in beer? One can say: Because vinegar is very strong, and due to its sharpness, it imparts an enhancing flavor, like with asafoetida. Or perhaps the creeping animal is small compared to the liquid, and if so, we should not prohibit it so much. And that is why he asked: What will be its fate?

Tosafot on Avodah Zarah 69a:1:2.hebrew: ההוא אימרטוטי אימרטט - יש לתמוה: עכשיו היאך אנו אוכלים דבש דבורים, והלא רגלי הדבורים מעורבים בדבש? ואף על גב דהוי פגם, מ"מ השרץ עצמו דאיפגם מיתסר לכ"ע. לכ"נ לר"ת דודאי רגלי הדבורים כיון דעצמות בעלמא נינהו, מותרים. דהא העצמות טהורים, דתנן במסכת (טהרות פרק א): "עצמות החמור טהורות", ורגלי הדבורים כעצמות החמור. והא דאמרינן: "אברים אין להם שיעור אפילו פחות מכזית מן המת ופחות מכעדשה מן השרץ", היינו לענין טומאה, וכגון דאיכא בשר עלויה. הא לאו הכי, טהורין. ולענין אכילה, שפיר דמי:
Tosafot on Avodah Zarah 69a:1:2.english: That one was dismembered - It is astonishing: How do we eat bee honey now? Are not bee legs mixed in the honey? And even though it is a detrimental flavor, nevertheless the creeping animal itself, which is detrimental, is forbidden to everyone. Therefore, it seems to Rabbeinu Tam that certainly bee legs, since they are mere bones, are permitted. For bones are pure, as we learned in Tractate Tahorot (Chapter 1): "The bones of a donkey are pure," and bee legs are like donkey bones. And that which we say: "Limbs have no minimum measure, even less than an olive-sized amount from a corpse and less than a lentil-sized amount from a creeping animal," this is concerning impurity, and when there is flesh on them. But if not so, they are pure. And concerning eating, it is certainly permitted:

Tosafot on Avodah Zarah 69a:2:1.hebrew: סבר לשעורי בק"א, אמר: לא גרע מתרומה כו' - תימה: נהי דתרומה נינהו, כשהוא בקדרה בדבר לח בטלה בס'. כדאמר פרק גיד הנשה (חולין דף צז.): "קדירה שבשל בה תרומה, לא יבשל בה חולין, ואם בשל בנותן טעם". וי"ל דס"ל: כיון שטעמו חזק בשכר, יש לדמותו לתרומה לדבר יבש. וא"ת: אמאי לא בטיל באחד ומאתים כמו ערלה וכלאי הכרם? וי"ל דשאני התם משום דהוו איסור הנאה, לכך לא ילפינן מיניה שרצים דשרו בהנאה, אבל תרומה שרי בהנאה:
Tosafot on Avodah Zarah 69a:2:1.english: He thought to calculate it at 101, he said: It is not worse than teruma, etc. - It is astonishing: Granted that it is teruma, when it is in a pot with a liquid, it is nullified by 60, as stated in the chapter Gid HaNashe (Hullin page 97a): "A pot in which teruma was cooked, one should not cook non-sacred food in it, and if one cooked, it is forbidden if it imparts flavor." One can say that he holds: Since its taste is strong in beer, it should be compared to teruma in a dry item. And if you ask: Why is it not nullified by 200, like orla and diverse kinds of the vineyard? One can say that there it is different because they are prohibitions of benefit, therefore we do not derive from them creeping animals, which are permitted for benefit. But teruma is permitted for benefit:

Tosafot on Avodah Zarah 69a:2:2.hebrew: כתבלין ופלפלין דלא בטיל טעמייהו - לא בס' ולא בק', שהרי מעט תבלין נותן טעם בקדרה גדולה. אבל אין לומר דלא בטיל כלל, דהא בהדי נותן טעם חשבינן ליה ולא בהדי אוסרין במשהו. כדקאמר לעיל (עבודה זרה דף סו.): "תבלין של שלשה שמות אסור ומצטרף" כו':
Tosafot on Avodah Zarah 69a:2:2.english: Like spices and peppers whose flavor is not nullified - Not by 60 nor by 100, for a small amount of spice imparts flavor in a large pot. But one cannot say that it is not nullified at all, for we consider it among those that impart flavor, and not among those that prohibit with any amount. As stated above (Avodah Zarah page 66a): "Spices of three names are forbidden and combine," etc.:

Tosafot on Avodah Zarah 69a:3:1.hebrew: שיער בחלא בחמשין - תימה: מ"ש דלעיל רוצה להחמיר בו אפילו יותר מס' וק', וכאן מיקל בו? וי"ל: משום דקסבר דבחלא לא אשבח כ"כ כמו בשיכרא:
Tosafot on Avodah Zarah 69a:3:1.english: He calculated it at fifty in vinegar - It is astonishing: What is the difference that above he wants to be stringent with it even more than 60 and 100, and here he is lenient with it? One can say: Because he holds that in vinegar, it does not enhance the flavor as much as in beer:

Tosafot on Avodah Zarah 69a:4:1.hebrew: אידי ואידי - פירוש: בשיכרא וחלא בשיתין. בהלכות גדולות ובירושלמי קאמר דשרץ לא בטיל כי אם באלף, ותלמודינו עיקר דבטל בששים כשאר איסורים:
Tosafot on Avodah Zarah 69a:4:1.english: This and that - Meaning, in beer and vinegar, by sixty. In Halakhot Gedolot and in the Jerusalem Talmud, it says that a creeping animal is not nullified except by a thousand, but our Talmud is primary, that it is nullified by sixty, like other prohibitions:
